issues.description: Preview API complects identity, value, and time by attaching a callable to the node
issues.detail: A node is an identity (a named step in a pipeline). A preview is a value (a snapshot of facts at some time). Stapling preview_fn onto the node object complects the structural identity of the pipeline step with a presentation-time callable that has nothing to do with the computation. The docs should at least name that the preview is a value computed at a different time than the node executes, and that node.preview() is a separate temporal event from node.run() — otherwise users will reach for closures to smuggle data across that time boundary (which the docs then encourage).

issues.description: Closure pattern for 'data context' is place-oriented programming dressed as functional style
issues.detail: The 'Use closure to capture context' example tells users to bake a sample_data list into the preview_fn at pipeline-construction time. That sample is now frozen at pipeline-build time, but the node will run later against different data. The doc presents this as the solution without naming the time mismatch: the preview will lie about the run. Either say 'preview reflects build-time facts, not run-time facts' explicitly, or point at the actual mechanism (read the dataset at preview time). Right now it teaches users to complect build-time values with run-time identities.

issues.description: Seven preview classes where one map of {kind, content, meta} would do
issues.detail: JsonPreview, TablePreview, PlotlyPreview, MermaidPreview, ImagePreview, TextPreview, CustomPreview all wrap a content field and an optional meta dict. This is the canonical case of using types where data would do: the kind is itself a value (a keyword/tag), and dispatch on it belongs at the renderer, not in the type system. The doc is locking users into seven import paths and seven constructors that all carry the same shape. A single Preview value with an explicit :kind would be simpler, serialise more naturally (the to_dict() call already flattens it), and would not need a CustomPreview escape hatch — every preview would already be 'custom' by virtue of its renderer_key. The docs should at minimum acknowledge that these are tags over the same shape.

issues.description: meta is overloaded: general metadata and renderer config share one bag
issues.detail: The doc explicitly says meta serves two purposes: contextual info (timestamps, versions) and rendering configuration (Mermaid layout, syntax language). These are two different concerns being complected into one untyped dict, and the docs admit it. Users now have to know which keys are inert metadata and which keys are load-bearing for the renderer. Splitting these (e.g. meta vs render_config, or namespacing keys) would separate 'facts about the preview' from 'instructions to the renderer.' At minimum, document the reserved keys per preview type.

issues.description: preview() returns an object that you immediately call to_dict() on — the object is incidental
issues.detail: The Basic Usage block shows `preview = training_node.preview()` followed immediately by `preview.to_dict()` for APIs/frontends. If the consumer always needs the dict, the object is incidental complexity sitting between the function and the wire format. Either the contract is 'preview returns data' (return the dict, drop the class) or 'preview returns a rich object with behavior' (justify the behavior). The docs should pick one and not show users that the first thing to do with the returned value is unwrap it.

issues.description: Mermaid example uses raw string content with embedded styling — escapes the type system entirely
issues.detail: MermaidPreview.content is a triple-quoted Mermaid DSL string, including `style A fill:#e1f5ff` directives mixed in with the graph topology. That is two concerns (structure of the diagram, visual styling) complected inside an opaque string blob that the preview type cannot inspect. This is fine as a thin pass-through, but the docs should be honest that MermaidPreview is essentially a TextPreview with a renderer hint — not a structured diagram type. Otherwise users will expect it to validate or transform their diagrams, and it won't.

issues.description: ImagePreview accepts URL or data URI in the same field with no discriminator
issues.detail: ImagePreview.content can be either an external URL or an inline base64 data URI, distinguished only by string prefix. These are two different values (a reference to a remote place vs. an inline value) sharing one slot. The docs note both options in a commented-out alternative but don't acknowledge the trust, caching, and time semantics differ wildly between them. At least flag that a URL is an identity pointing to something that may change, while a data URI is a value frozen at preview time.

issues.description: Best practices reads like an apology for the design
issues.detail: 'Keep previews lightweight', 'make previews fast', 'avoid expensive computations', 'handle errors with try-except', 'test preview functions' — every one of these is a workaround for the fact that preview_fn is an arbitrary callable invoked at an undefined time by an undefined caller, with no contract about cost, purity, or failure mode. The right answer is not a bulleted list of warnings; it is a clearer contract: 'preview functions must be pure, must not perform I/O without an explicit dataset accessor, and may raise PreviewError.' The docs should state the contract, not the etiquette.

issues.description: Experimental warning is correct but quiet about what 'experimental' costs the user
issues.detail: The warning says the feature may change or be removed. Fine. But the docs then teach seven concrete import paths, a closure pattern, and a renderer_key convention as if they were settled. If this is experimental, the doc should call out which surfaces are likely to change (the seven-class taxonomy, the meta overloading, the renderer_key contract) so users can make informed coupling decisions. Right now 'experimental' is a one-line disclaimer above a fully prescriptive tutorial.

review.summary: The docs accurately describe a feature that is itself complected: the node (an identity in the pipeline graph) now also carries a presentation-time callable, and the preview surface offers seven near-identical classes where a single tagged value would do. The closure pattern for "data context" silently teaches users to freeze build-time values inside run-time identities — a textbook time confusion that will produce previews that lie about runs. The `meta` field openly serves two unrelated jobs (contextual metadata and renderer configuration), and the Best Practices section reads as etiquette compensating for an under-specified contract around purity, cost, and failure. The documentation itself is clear and competent; the underlying API it documents is EASY-NOT-SIMPLE — familiar OO-flavored shapes that the docs would do well to at least name as experimental in their structure, not just their stability. The question that should have been asked first: is a preview a value the node produces, or a separate function over the node's identity — and once we answer that, do we need seven classes or one?
